speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all members of the house have followed with concern reports of the fighting now being conducted on India's northern frontiers against the communist Chinese invasion of India.
Despite determined resistance, Indian forces have had to withdraw. In the northwest frontier area, in the Ladakh district of Kashmir, the situation at the moment appears to be relatively stable though strong Chinese attacks are being directed toward the capture of an important Indian air field at Chushul. In the northeast frontier area, however, between Bhutan and Burma, the Chinese have delivered two massive attacks, moving beyond Walong near the Burmese border and pressing south of the Se La pass near the Bhutan border.
The result of this Chinese offensive has been to bring their troops to within 30 miles of the Assam plains, a part of India of great economic value and importance. In these plains flows the great Brahmaputra river, which is a vital factor in the lives of the people of northeast India, and also for the people of East Pakistan. In these grave circumstances we would all wish to assure once more the Indian people and the Indian army of our support for their determination to defeat aggression, and our sympathy for the losses they have suffered.
We have given, and intend to give, practical evidence of our support for India at this time. As I stated to the house on November 5, we have dispatched six DC-3 Dakota transport aircraft in answer to an urgent Indian request. These aircraft were flown out by R.C.A.F. aircrews and are now in India. Over the week end we received, through the Canadian high commissioner in New Delhi, more specific advice from the Indian government about their needs for further assistance in the form of aircraft, clothing for their forces
and other materials. In the light of this additional information the government is at the moment urgently considering how we can best meet the Indian government's requests and the most expeditious way by which our assistance can be sent to India.
There is one other factor in the present situation which derives from the fact that the great and populous subcontinent, part of whose borders has been penetrated, is shared by two commonwealth countries, India and Pakistan. The long standing differences between India and Pakistan over Kashmir have been a cause of regret to Canada and the other commonwealth countries for many years. We cherish a deep fraternal regard for both countries and have tried over the years to find means to reconcile their differences.
In the present circumstances, when communist Chinese aggression has forced India into a bloody conflict, the entire subcontinent, home of both India and Pakistan, is exposed to a grave threat. We would hope that this ominous situation might give new impetus to the search for a settlement between these two fellow members of the commonwealth. Such a settlement would facilitate a concentration of effort against the invading forces on the northern frontier; and I want to make this clear, that if there is anything Canada can do to further such a settlement, the Canadian government will respond wholeheartedly.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the information which the Prime Minister has been good enough to give the house makes it clear that the situation which now confronts India is a tragic one, as she faces aggression from China across her borders. It is also a strange situation in that there seems to be war in everything except the formal declaration of it. While this massive assault is being made on India, because that apparently is what it is, I gather diplomatic and trade relationships between the two countries have been maintained.
Of course this situation may change, and if it does change and India becomes not only the actual but the formal victim of aggression, then India's friends will have to reexamine their own relationships with the aggressor. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, this would be particularly true if the matter were brought before the United Nations and a decision in regard to aggression was taken there. There

Statement on Position of India may be very good reasons why this matter has not been brought before the United Nations assembly or the security council up to the present time, but I have noted, as no doubt the Prime Minister and others have noted, that tentative efforts have been made already on the part of some United Nations members to see whether it is possible to use the assembly or the security council for mediatory purposes. Perhaps that will be possible in the days ahead.
The Prime Minister mentioned-and I am glad he did, because it has a bearing on this situation-the relations between India and her neighbour and colleague in the commonwealth, Pakistan. It seems to me a very sad situation indeed when uncertainty on the oorder between these two friendly countries is such that apparently the Indian government is unable to move certain forces from that area to help repel the aggressor. If the Indian government could give an assurance to the Pakistan government that would be accepted that in moving these forces to meet the aggression, any additional equipment received would never be used against Pakistan, and if Pakistan in its turn could give an assurance that there would be no danger to India as a result of these forces being moved for the purpose of meeting the aggressor, that could be an important move toward peace on the part of these two countries and toward meeting the aggression. So I was very glad to hear the Prime Minister speak on that subject in the way he did.

Mr. Speaker, we are indebted to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) for keeping us informed about the serious and explosive situation which now exists in India and also for asserting that Canada will do everything possible not only to help establish peace in India, now attacked by communist China, but especially to bring about unity between two member countries of the commonwealth of nations, Pakistan and India.

The right hon. Prime Minister assures us that Canada will spare no effort to bring about unity between those two countries. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house and the people of Canada are deeply concerned about the setbacks which have been suffered by the Indian forces at the hands of the Chinese who have been carrying on a campaign of unprovoked aggression on the Indian border. I am sure also the country will be glad to hear the assurance given by the Prime Minister that Canada will give every possible aid to India.
I hope the Prime Minister will, if not today then on some subsequent occasion, tell the house just how tangible is this assistance. I understand that the Indian government were very anxious some time ago to get Caribou planes. Maybe it is not feasible to get these planes to them at this time. Certainly the house would like to know, and I think the people of Canada would like to know, that every available commodity and whatever military equipment which is in our possession and which is needed by the government of India will be made available to them as quickly as possible.
I think also people will be encouraged by the statement of the Prime Minister with reference to the members of the commonwealth seeking to give all the assistance they can in trying to settle the dispute between Pakistan and India. At the present time, my information is that some of the best units of the Indian army are being tied up on the border of Pakistan and that the government of Pakistan, rather than being enthusiastic about outside military aid being supplied to India, is concerned lest at some future date this military aid should be turned against her. This makes it imperative that some settlement be brought about, either by members of the commonwealth acting as mediators or by having the matter brought before the United Nations where it was before, but later dropped because of the refusal of India to agree to a plebiscite.
The other point raised concerns the position Canada should take with reference to the aggressor nation in this dispute. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, there may be good reasons why this question has not been brought before the United Nations. It may be that as long as this was simply a border dispute there were no grounds for bringing it before that body. However, if this attack is now a full scale invasion it seems to me that Canada should be pressing for the submission of this matter to the United

Nations so that if any action is to be taken it may be taken on an international basis. Canada is carrying on a considerable trade with China, and I think for Canada herself to take unilateral action would have little effect. I feel sure that the Canadian people and this House of Commons would back the government in supporting an international move toward economic sanctions if the United Nations felt this would be an effective means of deterring the aggressor.

speechtext:
In view of the fact that the advertisements for Canada savings bonds

Sales of Savings Bonds expired on November 15, I should like to make a short statement in connection therewith.
I am pleased to report to the house that recorded sales of Canada savings bonds up to and including Friday, November 16 were $1,350 million. A matter of special satisfaction to me is that this amount involved nearly 1,470,000 individual orders. The dollar total is 65 per cent higher than was recorded at the same time last year, and the number of orders is 28 per cent higher. Such a widespread sale is clear indication that Canada savings bonds are indeed the preferred investment by a wide margin for thrifty Canadian citizens in every walk of life.
I am equally pleased to be able to report that reported sales as of the same date through the payroll savings plan are $217 million. This is 2 per cent ahead of reported sales in this category last year, which hon. members may recall ultimately produced an alltime record of $223 million. The number of individual transactions involved totals 637,000, and the average payroll purchase amounted to over $340 as compared to the average purchase of $333 last year. I have no doubt that when final figures are available, this year's payroll savings sales will establish a new high mark by a comfortable margin.
It is appropriate that at this time I should extend my congratulations and appreciation to those who have made these splendid results possible. In particular I want to express appreciation to the thousands of voluntary payroll canvassers who enabled fellow employees to make the most of the payroll savings plan. I also extend this appreciation to the many hundreds of employers who willingly provided the necessary facilities and displayed enthusiasm and leadership in seeing that the campaign was well carried out.
Appreciation is also well merited by editors and operators of radio and T.V. stations who kept the public fully informed of the importance of the offering, of the advantages of purchase and of the progress of the campaign. Finally, 1 should also include in this appreciation the various sales agents and their employees who were responsible for the major proportion of total sales and who worked hard and efficiently to deal with the flood of orders that crossed their counters.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make about what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) just stated, but I regret that my observations will not have the same tenor as his.

The Minister of Finance is pleased with the increased sales of the Canadian government bonds. But every time he gets money from the people by selling them bonds, it means that less funds will be invested in the development of the country. He is getting money merely to add to our debt but not to invest in the future of Canada.
That is why I am not as pleased as the Minister of Finance to note such an increase in the sale of bonds.
Besides, another reason why I am not so very happy about those bond sales, is that those who buy them will have to pay taxes to repay those bonds and the interests involved. Finally, the people will have nothing to gain in the process, because they will pay taxes.
Mr. Speaker, a remarkable thing about the sale of those bonds is that businessmen are more interested in investing in the country's debt than in its assets. That is to say, they prefer to invest in the national debt rather than in the development of industry and trade.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not claim to be the father of this bill, although I am happy to sponsor it in the House of Commons. The proposed measure, sir-and I will be brief in my explanatory remarks of the bill- is a co-operative effort of Senator Roebuck, the chairman of the divorce committee in the Senate, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), who was chairman of the committee on miscellaneous private bills, and Mr. Hopkins and Dr. Ollivier, parliamentary counsel of the Senate and of the house respectively. Its purpose is to provide that the Senate may, on petition, by a resolution declare that a marriage is dissolved or annulled, as the case may be.
The advantage of this proposal is that it would avoid introducing a separate legislative measure for each and every divorce petition. As far as the House of Commons is concerned it would free this chamber from the burden of having those bills go through three readings and, more especially, through the miscellaneous private bills committee stage. Provision is made in the present bill for the passage of an act annulling or modifying such resolution under certain conditions, such as within a certain period of time, for the protection of respondents and co-respondents.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, if the minister does not wish to speak, I do. It does seem to me that merely for the convenience of the taxpayers, if one were considering no other principle at all, it would be desirable to have these far reaching changes in the law passed by parliament; and merely for the convenience of the taxpayers it would be desirable for them to know, surely, that the taxes they were being asked to pay had been reviewed carefully by their representatives in parliament.
We did have-and I do not like to keep coming back to the lobsters which made the face of the Minister of Finance rather red- evidence that some of these things that were done on June 24 were rather inadvertent, or accidental, or were not quite what the government really intended. If the representatives of the people were given the opportunity -as I submit, sir, would be desirable-in considering this bill to review all the changes in the Customs Tariff, that would have been less likely to happen. I do not say that parliament does not occasionally overlook some things even in bills, but it is less likely to happen if there is such a review. I say this with experience of about the same length as the Minister of Finance in the cabinet. should have adopted another principle in amendment of the Excise Tax Act, that of reducing excise taxes instead of the tax with which it has dealt.
Then the Speaker went on to give ancillary reasons for his ruling, but it seems to me what I have quoted deals with the question whether an amendment of this kind can be moved. This view is supported by citation No. 382 of Beauchesne's fourth edition:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill to move as an amendment to the question-
And this applies, as Your Honour knows, to the third reading also-
-a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction or prosecution .. .
It seems to me that the amendment does fulfil the requirements of that citation. In other words the amendment has to be related to the bill but not amend a part of the bill or something which was capable of being a part of the bill; because, if it were that, it could be moved in committee and therefore could not be moved in a motion which was opposed to proceeding with the measure.
It seems to me I should not take any more of Your Honour's time, because these two citations would appear to be conclusive.

Perhaps I may speak on the point of order and, more particularly, deal with the argument which has just been made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who in my submission has somewhat twisted the meaning of citation 382 in Beauchesne. I think it is clear on reading that citation that it has reference to things which may happen on second reading of the bill. On second reading, as we know, we are concerned with whether the house accepts or rejects the principle of a bill. I submit this citation has no relevance to any motions which may be made on third reading, where the debate and the type of motion permissible are much more restricted.
The second point I should like to make is that in effect we have here an expanded negative that the bill be not now read a third time, and setting forth one reason why it should not. No matter how the hon. member argues his point, I submit this is still an expanded negative and, as such, at variance

with our practice. Further, I might point out that at page 289 of Beauchesne various examples are given of instances where Speakers in the past have declared similar motions to be out of order, and I think the hon. members' motion follows within this category.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I in half a sentence congratulate the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on presenting a much more rational amendment today than we had from him yesterday.
When the hon. member, a moment ago, read from citation 382 of Beauchesne, the citation which indicates what can be done by way of amendment to the motion for second reading, he said, paraphrasing another citation, that the same things can, of course, be done on third reading.
I think it would be useful to read the sentence from citation 418 which confirms what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, even though there are certain restrictions. The key sentence is:
All amendments which may be moved on a second reading of a bill may be moved on the third reading with the restriction that they cannot deal with any matter which is not contained in the bill.
The hon. member who spoke a moment ago said there is a difference between second reading and third reading. There is a difference, but it is right there; the restriction is that an amendment to the motion for third reading must deal with matters that are contained in the bill.
I submit that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has done precisely that. He has limited his reasons for not wanting to give third reading of the bill now to matters which are in the bill. He moves that this bill be not read a third time until surcharges approved by order in council which alter rates set up in this bill are considered by the house. We know from the discussion we had in committee of the whole that there are certain rates in this bill which are altered by surcharges approved by order in council, or vice versa. So the amendment clearly states two things which are in the bill itself. Therefore it seems to me that the argument about relevancy is well met by the way in which this amendment is framed.
There is no question but that certain types of amendments are in order on third reading, and if I had time to look it up I think I could find the answer to the expanded negative. There are times when even that is permissible. It is permissible to move that a bill be not now read a second time or a third time even though that is a negative, particularly when reasons are given for so moving.
The example to which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate referred I find very

interesting. When Mr. Speaker Michener ruled on the motion of the hon. member for Fort William on July 30, 1958, that was a case of a member asking for third reading not to take place until certain other things had been done. That is precisely what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is asking for. He is keeping it within the compass of the bill itself. The motion talks of rates set by the bill. The motion talks of the act which this bill amends. I submit that he has not gone astray, that the amendment is in order, and that it should be put to the house as such.

Mr. Speaker, in the debate yesterday -I think it was in committee and perhaps you were not present-it was admitted by the Minister of Finance that included in the schedule to this bill are items that bear a surcharge imposed by order in council. This was done subsequent to the budget resolutions of April 10. The point being raised here is that we are not dealing realistically with the rates shown in this schedule if we do not concern ourselves with what is superimposed upon these rates, namely the effect on the taxpayer of the surcharges imposed by the June 24 order in council which the Prime Minister said involved $200 million of taxation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this question is one which deserves very serious consideration. It is the first time this session that an amendment has been moved on third reading, and we must be rather careful as to what course is followed in this regard. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has already quoted citation 418 on page 288 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. That citation says:
All amendments which may be moved on a second reading of a bill may be moved on the third reading with the restriction that they cannot deal with any matter which is not contained in the bill.
The point has already been made by the Minister of Finance that surcharges are not contained in the bill. Then further down in the citation it says:
When a motion is made "that the bill be now read a third time'', the same kind of amendments are permissible as on the second reading...
-that is, amendments postponing second reading for three or six months, and specific examples of the type of amendment that Mr. Beauchesne had in mind when he was writing that paragraph are given. Mr. Speaker, if you will refer to Bourinot, fourth edition, pages
Customs Tariff
528 and 529, you will find there a dissertation dealing with amendments on third reading. I quote from page 528:
In the Senate it is usual to follow the English practice and amend the bill, when necessary, on consideration of the bill as amended in committee of the whole.
That is, when third reading stage is reached.
As a fact the Canadian Commons never amend the bill at this stage in accordance with the English practice. It is quite usual, however, for a member to move that the order for consideration be discharged and the bill committed for the purpose of amending the bill in any particular.
Based on that practice in the House of Commons, which practice has been followed since, an hon. member might suggest in his amendment that the bill be recommitted to the committee for amendment according to the lines he has in mind. To reinforce that citation I refer to May's sixteenth edition, page 578, which deals with the subject of amendments on third reading. This matter is dealt with as follows:
By standing order No. 53-
That is the English standing order.
-verbal amendments only can now be made to a bill on the third reading. If material amendments are desired, the order for the third reading of the bill should be discharged, and the bill recommitted to allow the introduction of the amendments in committee. In such cases it has been customary to consider the bill, as amended on recommittal, and to read it the third time immediately.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that these citations indicate that the method of procedure on third reading differs from the method of procedure on second reading; and when we reach third reading, if amendments are desired, the bill would be recommitted to the committee stage where the amendments would be put forward. But this is not the case of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who simply is attempting to give a disguised six months' hoist to the bill by the use of his phrase about the surcharges being presented to the house for consideration. It is a disguised six months' hoist. It would have been better if he had moved his amendment in the proper manner. But based on these references, Mr. Speaker, I say that the amendment is entirely out of order.

Customs Tariff

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether what I have to say is absolutely new. I wanted to make some comment on a point or two made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I think the minister attempted to put forward the idea that there was something irregular in moving a reasoned amendment on third reading. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has already referred to Beauchesne, and I have the parliamentary dictionary by Abraham and Hawtrey in my hand which has been used as an authority in this house on previous occasions by Mr. Speaker Michener. On page 162 the following appears:
A reasoned amendment may be moved on second or third reading of a bill, and on certain other occasions as stated below.
This is a reasoned amendment because it gives the reason why the house should not proceed with the third reading of the bill. It is in an entirely different category from a six months' hoist, which is a delaying amendment and not a reasoned amendment. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate could easily have moved a delaying amendment, but he chose to move a reasoned amendment because he wished to assert a principle in connection with the passage of the bill through the house. The Minister of Veterans Affairs said that this amendment was irregular because there was no reference in the bill itself to surcharges. That is perfectly true, but the amendment is made relevant to the bill because of the reference in the bill to tariff rates. This provides the link of relevancy between the amendment and the bill itself.
In my judgment the category into which this amendment falls is found in Sir Erskine May's sixteenth edition, page 530, where the author establishes three categories of reasoned amendments. Category No. 2 is an amendment expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with the introduction or prosecution of a bill, and the circumstance to which we object in the prosecution of this bill is that surcharges which affect the rates contained in the bill have not been brought before parliament for consideration.

Would the hon. member permit a question at this stage? Would he draw the attention of the house to the fact that on page 530 of May, to which he referred, the general heading is "Amendment

to Question for Second Reading". There is no reference to third reading at all.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is no question there. In a more limited way an amendment may be advanced at third reading which could have been advanced at second reading. On the question of a reasoned amendment, I would put it to hon. members that the fact that an amendment is a reasoned amendment does not give it, shall we say, a free ticket. Therefore, even though it may be a reasoned amendment it may lose out on other grounds. I think that disposes entirely of the arguments with regard to whether or not this is a reasoned amendment. Even if it is, that does not necessarily let it in.
In considering the amendment as put before me, I would refer first of all to citation 418 in Beauchesne where we see that the second sentence reads as follows:
All amendments which may be moved on a second reading of a bill may be moved on the third reading with the restriction that they cannot deal with any matter which is not contained in the bill.
Here the question is whether there is any distinction between surcharges and any matters found within the bill. In the bill there are amendments to rates. An amendment setting forth a proposition dealing with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion is not relevant and cannot be moved.
I thank all hon. members for what they have said, but with the greatest respect I am of the opinion that surcharges are not rates within the meaning of the Customs Tariff act. Surcharges are something ancillary and not generally applied. They are removable by order. They are of an entirely different category and therefore they are not a matter referred to within the bill. There is a clear distinction in my mind between surcharges and the customs rates set out in the bill under consideration as well as in the Customs Tariff act.
In addition, I think the amendment would be out of order on a second basis in that in effect it is an expanded negative and so is contrary to the sense of the main motion. Therefore I cannot accept the amendment.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I would say to my hon. friend for Essex East, who was so erroneous on every fact he stated this afternoon that you would have thought he was in a trance, that when Mr. Abbott was minister of finance and made his tariff changes, there was not even an order in council passed when the tariff changes were made by radio.
Of course not, there was a bill before parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend would mind the advice of the Speaker and keep quiet, it would help. He has been inaccurate enough this afternoon, and surely he should not be wrong in his procedure as well. I do not think he made an accurate statement in connection with this whole matter.
Mr. Speaker, just what happened on that occasion? When the Canadian people, either inadvertently or just by chance, turned on the radio on that night, they heard the then minister of finance saying: "Hereafter you are going to pay X per cent more excise tax on every item which you buy". That was done by radio; and the hon. member says it was implemented by parliament and implemented by order in council. Do you know what happened, Mr. Speaker? That very night the deputy minister of customs and excise, who is still deputy minister, sent out wires to every officer in Canada telling them to impose that tax as from midnight that night. That was something done by radio and then by telegram. And there was no order in council-
There was a bill put before parliament.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There was no order in council at any time. There was not even an act by the executive. What it was was an act by radio waves, and that is all. It was a miracle from heaven which told the people, if they happened to turn on their radios, that on that night, or the next night, I presume, what these charges were to be. Mr. Speaker, these

Customs Tariff
are the gentlemen who protest that parliament has been wronged and that their rights have been interfered with.
They also said that parliament was called to confirm that measure. Parliament was not called to confirm it. That made it all the worse.
It was, two weeks after.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, parliament had been called before this voice came out over the air saying what the new taxes would be. But the minister of finance of that day, despite the fact that parliament had been called -not to consider these taxation matters, but had been called in the regular course of events -with parliament just over the horizon, could not wait for parliament to be assembled. He could not wait to submit his proposals to parliament, but in the middle of the night, by radio, while members of parliament were almost packing to come here, he imposed this taxation. And so when we are told that (a) there was an order in council, that is wrong; and when we are told (b) that parliament was called to confirm it, that is also wrong. This was done despite parliament and in contempt of parliament. Parliament met and debated various matters. Matters were adjourned and discussed. I have read Hansard and have the record, and it was not until weeks after that parliament assembled, I am certain after the Easter recess, that this matter was finally brought before it.
So that when we are told by this member that this is something which is wrong and contrary to parliamentary principles, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is at least one precedent in this matter which I am sure my hon. friends opposite will find it very hard to deny, in comparison with which this government, in following legislative authority laid down by statute and established by parliament, is in certainly a much better position, and in a perfectly proper legal position.
I was glad to hear my hon. friend say, and I agree with him, that the term "surcharges" has somehow inadvertently got, I think, into the title of the order in council, because it is the only place it appears. This is a matter dealing with tariff rates; the British preferential, the most favoured nation, and the general tariff. There is no reference per se whatsoever to surcharges except in the title of the order in council which was passed. Again I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this order in council was in accordance with parliamentary authority, not only the imposition of it but also in the relieving section which is provided for under the Financial Administration Act. I can speak with some experience
[Mr. NowlanJ	fjf[
as minister of national revenue, Mr. Speaker. I know that you never heard of any of these matters during the course of the last four or five years you served in the other parliament, but there were scores and scores of times when the then minister of national revenue, through treasury board on recommendation, relieved taxation, and permitted rebates. There were also times when taxation abatements were suspended and taxation imposed again. All those matters have been done by order in council. There is nothing unusual about these procedures whatsoever. This is a matter of practice which has come down through the years in our parliamentary association. It is one which has been recognized by all governments and by both of the parties which have formed governments in this country since confederation. I rather resent, Mr. Speaker, the suggestion that there is something wrong, immoral, improper, arbitrary, and in defiance of parliament, in what we have done.
Mr. Speaker, as I have said, there will be plenty of opportunities to raise this matter in parliament. I can assure my hon. friends that when my estimates come before the house they can go into the matter in any detail in which they see fit. As far as I am concerned, I would be prepared to answer any and every question in connection with the application and the implication of surcharges on the tariff structure of this country. the second reading of Bill No. S-7, to incorporate the Christian Brothers of Ireland in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to thank hon. members for their consideration in allowing me to bring forward this matter at this time. Out of consideration for this step on the part of the house I will not trespass unduly upon its time. I would commence by drawing the attention of hon. members to the peculiar position in which the Christian Brothers of Ireland in Canada find themselves on today's order paper. They have been in tight fixes before in Canada but never before have they found themselves isolated among 356 couples aspiring to be divorced. Indeed, one would have to look for the item on the order paper today with diligence and perseverance in order to find it. I assure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pick-ersgill), who is interested in the order of Christian brothers-

subtopic: CHRISTIAN BROTHERS OF IRELAND IN CANADA
speechtext: That is true.

subtopic: CHRISTIAN BROTHERS OF IRELAND IN CANADA
speechtext:
-because of their widespread activity in the province to which he now owes his patrimony, that I will not take an undue amount of time, so that he can return to the consideration of other matters representing, one might say, the other side of the coin of Christianity. I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that while the Christian Brothers of Ireland in Canada, who are seeking to incorporate themselves, would not approve of all of the other items under private bills today they would probably not wish me to stand in the way of that which parliament has said should be done.
This is essentially a very simple bill, Mr. Speaker. Hon. members will now have it at their places in both the French and English languages. It consists of 16 sections. It is in effect simply a bill whereby the order of Christian Brothers desires parliament to incorporate them under the title of The Christian Brothers of Ireland in Canada so that they may carry on the work of a religious body and be enabled to hold property, allowed to build and conduct schools and carry out the other objectives of their order.
I should say something about the order in Canada and its international ramifications. The order originated in Ireland and its founder was Edmund Ignatius Rice, one of seven children of a well known county Kilkenny family in southern Ireland. He was first apprenticed to his uncle who had a substantial business in Waterford in the county of Cork. The uncle was an exporter, importer and dealer in ships' provisions. This is an interesting point because the Christian Brothers of Ireland in Canada now have very extensive educational responsibilities in the province of Newfoundland. Indeed, with regard to this measure, which comes to us from the other place, again without a murmur of senatorial discontent, a recent distinguished appointee to that body said that the greatest blessings ever imported into Newfoundland were the order of Christian Brothers and rabbits. In the province of Newfoundland the Christian Brothers are continuing their historical connection with the sea and all her ways.
Edmund Rice, the founder of the order, inherited his uncle's business and became a successful businessman. He amassed what would in those days have been regarded as a modest fortune but his instincts were always greatly humanist and he desired to turn himself to the welfare of other people, particularly by the practice of religious avocations. There was a glaring lack of educational facilities for the poor boys of Waterford and, indeed, throughout Ireland generally.
The order was not easily founded but, like so many other teaching orders in Canada and other countries, both religious and lay, it owes much of its genesis, its strength and its vitality to the perseverance and Godfearing devotion of those who gave it its being and who have kept it alive. Times and ideas change and the winds of adversity which blew upon Edmund Rice in his younger years and upon his conception of a teaching order of Christian brothers calmed and ultimately stilled. Edmund Rice took advantage of the change in attitude of the Irish people and with the approval of his bishop decided to form the members of the small community who had gathered about him into a society consecrated by vows to the service of God and religion.
In 1808 the congregation of the brothers of the Christian schools of Ireland was informally founded. Twelve years later, by brief of Pope Pius VII, the congregation was formally established and appropriately Edmund Rice became its first superior. The development of the order thereafter was rapid. Its schools spread throughout Ireland. Interesting in its history is the account of a great occasion in 1822 at North Richmond

Private Bills
street in Dublin when the cornerstone of the great O'Connell school was laid by the celebrated Daniel O'Connell in the presence of 100,000 people. On that occasion Daniel O'Connell referred to Edmund Rice, who had become Brother Edmund Rice, as "the patriarch of the monks of the west".
The order now has 12 schools throughout Canada. Two are located in Vancouver, one in Victoria, one in Montreal and eight in the province of Newfoundland. The total membership of the order of Christian brothers in Canada today is approximately 140 and they have in their trust the education of 10,000 pupils. One of their first schools in Canada was St. Mary's college, now the great Jesuit University of St. Mary's in Halifax. I hope that hon. members will not hold it against the purposes sought by the Christian brothers in this bill that the humble sponsor of it in this chamber is himself an alumnus of St. Mary's University. Indeed, the hon. and friendly parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is another graduate of Christian brothers' teaching.
Had I not been in the position this afternoon of interrupting the meditation of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on such things as 302 bills for the relief of one from another, I would have trespassed at greater length upon the time of the house to relate some anecdotes which I think would illustrate the great faith and the great humanity of the order of Christian brothers.
The purpose of the bill before us is essentially a very simple one. At the present time there is one provincialate of the Christian Brothers of Ireland which serves the whole of the North American continent. The bill before us provides for the promotion of a Canadian provincialate with its head office in the city of Montreal or, as hon. members will see in section 2 of the bill, in such other place in Canada as the corporation may from time to time determine by bylaw and publish in the Canada Gazette.
The objectives sought to be served by the statutory enactment incorporating the Christian Brothers of Ireland in Canada are set out in section 3. Essentially, they provide for the provision by the order of educational facilities, orphanages and novitiates; promotion of the religious life; the creation, erection, organization and administration of other educational institutions, such as colleges, schools and academies and the administration in Canada of the property, business and other temporal affairs of this religiously inclined order.
The bill thereafter, Mr. Speaker, contains the customary and predictable sections dealing with the incorporation of religious and

other bodies. It provides in section 4 for the maintenance of schools. The order desires to have the power to purchase land, to buy and sell property and indeed to finance itself by the borrowing of money.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, is one which has been considered in the other place. It will be referred now, if the house sees fit as I hope it will to give it second reading, to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills. The purpose, in summary, is very simple. The Christian Brothers of Ireland in Canada desire to be incorporated as such. They are now operating under a North American provincialate and they desire to have a Canadian provincialate. In order to do so, they have come to parliament seeking this act of incorporation. I thank hon. members of the house for their consideration of this bill in precedence to others this afternoon, and I recommend it earnestly and fervently and with recollected affection of the Christian Brothers to the consideration of this house.

Mr. Speaker, I only have a brief comment to make in respect of this particular bill because of some

peculiarities surrounding it. These peculiarities, I might say, are somewhat connected with the general argument which colleagues of mine were presenting on an earlier occasion in connection with another bill. In order to understand the background, I think we have to look at some parts of the petition to the Senate upon which this particular bill is founded. The pertinent reasons for the comments I am about to make are contained in the petition, parts numbers 6 and 7. There are three general comments. The first one is, and I shall quote rather than paraphrase to make sure it is correct:
That after the said marriage, your petitioner lived and cohabited with the said Jonathan Fayette Meakins and there are now living issue of the said marriage three (3) children: Jonathan Lar-month Meakins, born January 8, 1941; Sally Anne Meakins, born February 26, 1942; Sandra Diane Meakins, born December 25, 1945.
So, in addition to the question of whether or not the marriage should be dissolved as this bill seeks to do, we are, I believe, concerned with the effect of that dissolution upon the children of the marriage, especially in view of the fact that one of them is of the age of 16.
Paragraph No. 7 reads:
That on or about the 25th day of January, 1961, your petitioner instituted proceedings in the superior court of the province of Quebec sitting in and for the district of Montreal for a separation as to bed and board from her said husband, for custody of her children and for alimony.
There are two points here with which we must concern ourselves, namely the custody of the children and the alimony payments. Then, there is an indication as to what the support is, and I quote:
That on or about the 5th day of April, 1961, by judgment of Mr. Justice Maurice Cousineau, a judge of the superior court of the province of Quebec, your petitioner was granted a separation as to bed and board from her said husband, granted the custody of her said three minor children and granted an alimentary allowance of three hundred and seventy five dollars a month for herself and for the support of her said children as long as they are living with her . . .
Her husband was further ordered to pay the cost of the education and clothing of the said children, and any medical and dental expenses incurred for them.
There is reference following that to a marriage agreement entered into prior to the marriage, and I shall read from it as follows:
That by ante-nuptial contract entered into on the 2nd day of June, 1939 between your petitioner and her said husband, before notary George Lyman VanVliet of the city of Montreal, province of Quebec, her husband undertook to pay her the sum of twenty five thousand dollars ($25,000), which amount by agreement entered into between your petitioner and her said husband, her said husband will pay her the said sum if and when the marriage herein mentioned is dissolved, at which time
Private Bills-Divorce
your petitioner will have the legal capacity to discharge her said husband from his legal obligations undertaken in virtue of the terms of the said contract.
Therefore there are three points about which this parliament, and subsequently the miscellaneous private bills committee, must concern themselves: first, the custody of the children and their maintenance, second, the question of the payment of alimony to the wife, and third the payment of the lump sum of $25,000 referred to in the marriage contract of 1939.
As has been said earlier there are some rulings, which in my opinion are not too definite, to the effect that such things as the maintenance and custody of children and alimony to the wife are not the business of this parliament. In the past we have gone along with that view, more by reason of ignorance than anything else, but it appears we were in error and that they are things with which the parliament of Canada must concern itself. They are things which should be contained within the bill itself. It should contain more than the simple clause 1 which says:
The said marriage is hereby dissolved, and shall be henceforth null and void to all intents and purposes whatsoever.
This bill and others like it, which will become statutes of Canada, should contain a declaration relating to the maintenance of the children and their custody, and the payment of alimony to the wife. Unless we have such provisions within it we are only concerning ourselves with half of the problem or half of the difficulty, and it is incorrect to dissolve a marriage without taking steps to deal with these other all important questions.
I know the argument has been advanced that we cannot do this because these, in effect, are civil rights and are thereby matters which come within the jurisdiction of the provinces, in this case the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec; but there are within our party and in the house hon. gentlemen versed in the law, and in particular two hon. gentlemen who have studied this question in great detail and will be able to argue, far more forcibly than I, the reason why we must concern ourselves with these matters and why we are constitutionally correct in so concerning ourselves.
For the time being I would leave it at that. I have not given any lengthy recitations from the evidence itself, but may I merely say in passing that the evidence is there and that there was extensive questioning by hon. members of the Senate committee about such things as the children, their age, civil actions in Quebec relating to bed and board, and the ante-nuptial contract referred to in the

Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of this particular bill we are being asked to divorce this couple whose marriage, we are informed by document, took place in the province of Quebec. It is interesting to note that according to the bill the domicile is considered to be in Canada, although there is reference to the provincial domicile as well.
This is one of these cases where no settlement has been made, and also there were no previous proceedings in other courts to provide for financial arrangements between the petitioner and the respondent. We are also fortunate in this case that there are no children involved; but the fact that we are not given any guidance from the other place as to the settlement that will be arrived at to take care of the petitioner, seems to me to indicate a lack of something in our proceedings. I believe there should be a statement saying some arrangement has been made which will provide for the maintenance of this woman after the divorce is granted.
In examining the evidence we are impressed with the fact that in this case private detectives were not employed. The persons involved are relatives, which makes it a difficult case to discuss from the point of view that the people who are testifying are all connected with the case, and therefore some

of the contentions that are made in many of the cases where hotel and private detectives are used, are not necessarily applicable.
When this bill goes to the committee I would submit that the committee should examine it in the light of a settlement for the woman in this case, so that the committee will be assured that the lady will be looked after, because this divorce is the result of no fault of hers.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very brief comment to make on this bill. I am not going to go into great detail on this point, but it is something the miscellaneous private bills committee should consider. Two people appeared as witnesses on behalf of the petitioner, each of whom is a relative of the petitioner. Usually, as we have discovered from discussing these bills previously, when so-called private detectives or investigators appear as witnesses there are also two in number. Part of the comments of the presiding judge in a divorce case in Ontario was to this effect. He said that if there are witnesses who are not licensed to practise the profession, if that is what it can be called, of a private detective, the court which hears that particular case should give the testimony of those witnesses even greater scrutiny than it would if they were licensed detectives. The argument used by the court in that case was that people who are not licensed as private detectives, when they appear to give evidence on behalf of a petitioner in such a case are nothing more than paid witnesses, and this is especially so when witnesses are relatives of the petitioner.
I am not in any way attempting to indicate that in this particular case the two witnesses who appeared might, because of an emotional attachment to the family have coloured or flavoured their evidence, but this was the attitude taken by the judge in the case to which I referred but which I do not have with me at the moment. I merely asked that, by virtue of the fact that the two witnesses involved are apparently not licensed, or there is no indication that they are licensed as private detectives under the relevant Quebec statute, the committee should perhaps give a little more care to the consideration of the evidence given by those witnesses than might normally be the case or has been the case in divorce petitions.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this bill. In doing so I would like to make it clear that the only reason I wish to speak on this measure for the relief of Mrs. Bagry is to ask the house to provide adequate protection for the petitioner in its consideration of the bill. This bill asks us to dissolve a marriage which took place on May 8, 1945. Upon perusing the evidence it is clear that there are children of the marriage and that at least one of those children is under the age of 16 years.
It was suggested to the house that we must adequately exercise our legislative powers over divorce. Clearly under the statutes and under the law it is our duty to go into the whole matter of the children, their custody and maintenance. In perusing the evidence in this case it is clear, Mr. Speaker, that the history of this particular marriage is very unsatisfactory from the point of view of the children of the marriage. There were previous separations; the husband neglected for years to support the children, and he would appear and disappear. The whole matter of looking after the children has been very unsatisfactory. Of course, Mr. Speaker, once we exercise our legislative powers in dealing with the relief of this individual, the difficulty is that if we fail to properly take care of the custody of the children and the maintenance of the wife there is some doubt as to what will happen to any action which may have been taken in other courts. In effect, if we neglect to deal with the children and their welfare, we may leave a vacuum by virtue of the fact that in purporting to exercise our legislative power, and failing in fact to do so, we will wipe out any judgments which have been handed down by lower courts. By our very neglect in failing to carry out our legislative duties adequately we may be undoing anything which may have been done in the lower courts.
The other problem that occurs to me in relation to this bill demonstrates the absurdity of parliament dealing with these matters. It is, how are we going to enforce our edicts? Assuming that the House of Commons will accept the proposition that we simply
Private Bills-Divorce
must deal with the welfare of these children-and we do, in effect, in final passage of the bill, make provision for these children who are unable to look after themselves- how do we enforce that judgment in the event that the errant spouse decides to defy the will of parliament and neglects to keep up whatever order we may make? How do we discipline him? Do we have him brought before us periodically and chastise him and order him to carry out the terms of the bill? The whole procedure becomes an absurdity in itself, Mr. Speaker. Yet once we enter this whole field of divorce, which clearly under the British North America Act is given to parliament, we are forced into this ridiculous position of acting as a court over situations that we are just not adequately equipped to deal with.
For example, Mr. Speaker, there is no evidence before us of the circumstances under which these children live, have lived or will live. There is no evidence as to how adequately the husband can support them. We do not know what is his income. There is no way in which we as a parliament can properly and adequately deal with this matter, and yet we have the legislative duty to deal with it thrust upon us. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), when other bills were before the house, began to put the legal argument to hon. members, but since it has not been challenged there seems little point in repeating it. The legal case is strong and undisputed. Indeed, in my view and in the view of other hon. members of this party, the legal case is unassailable.
Once parliament is asked to legislate on matters of divorce it must take into account all the ancillary questions such as the welfare of the children in each case, the support of the children in the future, their education and so on. All these things must be brought before us. But, surely, it is becoming evident to hon. members that if we are really to carry out our legislative duties properly the parliament of Canada will be able to deal with little else but divorces in the time available. Presumably, there will be 700 or 800 of these cases before us eventually and we shall be placed in the position of needing to inquire into all the matters ancillary to the merits of each case. Surely, this should not be necessary. Surely, some provision could be enacted so as to remove this duty from parliament. We are not able to deal with it adequately. For one thing we do not have the information which we need. We shall do a poor job. We shall injure the parties to the application, we shall injure the children of the marriage

Private Bills-Divorce
and, no doubt, make it difficult for them to lead normal lives, all because we continue to legislate on questions of this kind.
It seems to me we should set up a royal commission to go into this whole matter-to discuss it from coast to coast, and eventually relieve parliament of a duty which it does not want and is not equipped to perform adequately.

It is very interesting to note in this petition that a number of changes have been made in the presentation. I would also draw the attention of the house to one paragraph in the original petition, paragraph 9, which states:
That there have been no previous proceedings instituted with reference to the marriage or any children thereof, including applications to the parliament of Canada, petitions and writs for divorce actions, alimony or maintenance, separation from bed and boards and the custody or maintenance of any children of the marriage, and there are no agreements of financial arrangements between the spouses with reference to the marriage or any children thereof.
I wonder whether the hon. member who moved this motion would not agree to move

an amendment in respect of this particular paragraph. It is my understanding that the bill before us was introduced in the Senate a year ago. In effect, this represents a reintroduction of the same bill' with certain notations attached to it at the insistence of the Senate. 1 believe the clause which I have quoted should be changed because the inference might be drawn from the evidence that the assurance given in the petition could be taken as saying that the case had not been before parliament on a previous occasion. I suggest the fact that this petition has been reintroduced in the Senate makes this particular paragraph of the petition not applicable this year and, therefore, not correct, having regard to the date on which it was made. This situation arises from the fact that certain protection has been given to those who wish to continue their applications on the basis of a previous application a year ago. It is my opinion that a notation should be attached to the bill to the effect that these petitioners have been asked whether or not they have decided to live together again during the period in which this petition has been before parliament; whether they have reconsidered the matter; and it might also say whether the people concerned are alive or dead. In my opinion this notation should be attached to the bill. If it is not, I believe the mover of this bill should withdraw it, or at least maintain a certain amount of correctness in its presentation.
It is also interesting to note that the petition continues along these lines:
Your petitioner therefore humbly prays that your honourable house will be pleased to pass an act dissolving the said marriage between your petitioner and the said-
I will leave out the name because it is very difficult to pronounce.
-and enabling your petitioner to marry again, and granting your petitioner such further and other relief in the premises as to your honourable house may seem meet.
I wonder whether in this particular case provision has been made particularly for the petitioner so that she will be looked after? The evidence indicates that she is the innocent party, and therefore I think we should give some consideration to that part of her petition which asks parliament to grant her not only a divorce but the other relief which we have the right to grant.
Mr. Speaker, several things were said in the original petition which were amended before counsel on January 29, 1962. The original petition was changed to 1959 from 1960. The one now before us has already had this change made, and in the presentation we have there is an amendment which 27507-3-116
Private Bills*-Divorce purports to be an actual copy of the amendment to the original petition made by the petitioner. I would suggest that the original, which has obviously been amended by the report given to the Senate in January, in which they asked for the deletion of 1960 and the substitution therefor of 1959, should be before us. I think that these changes should be made, because it seems to me that this is not a legal copy of the original petition as presented; it has been amended by members of the other place.
It is also interesting to note that we are asked to give relief to a lady now living in the province of British Columbia. Because domicile is rather provincial in scope and we have never given complete freedom to our womenfolk, there has been attached to them the domicile of their husbands. Even when they have left the bed and board of their husbands they are still considered to be domiciled in the province in which is their husband's domicile. In this case the petitioner has had to come from British Columbia to Ottawa to present her petition. I am not sure whether hon. members of the other place would have accepted this petition had it been impossible to present the petition without her appearing. This raises a problem where the wife has moved to another province as distant as British Columbia and has to come to Ottawa to present her petition. I think it would have been very interesting if the legal counsel for this lady had been from British Columbia. He was not; but if he had been and he had decided to come here to present this petition, with no respondent or corespondent-because they did not appear in this case-I wonder whether we are not asking a great deal from people who do move about from province to province to return to, say, the province of their husbands' domicile to make their presentation to parliament.
I suggest that this is another instance where a great deal of cost has been added which normally would not be the case; and I wonder whether it is not now time to give consideration to the passage in this bill which says that this lady resided in the city of Vancouver, in the province of British Columbia, and is the wife of so and so who is domiciled in Canada and resides at the city of Montreal, in the province of Quebec, and to strike out what the original bill refers to as her domicile being in the the province of Quebec, which would have allowed her, in my opinion, to present her petition in another province.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I mentioned at the close of the discussion last night that this amendment was to tidy up the legislation in connection with the matter of appraisal fees on which we have set limits. The suggestion was made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that we should put some provision in the clause to limit the amount of the supervising fee. At that time I said this was covered in the regulations and the amount was $25. He suggested at that time that we should amend the act by putting this regulation in the act itself. As far as I am concerned, it does not achieve anything for the farmers but it does not hurt the act by putting it in. It is just another rigidity, and if the committee wants an amendment I can move one. It is up to the committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
If there is really any difference, except for minor amendments between this legislation and the former farm loan board legislation, it would appear to be mainly in the field of the supervision of credit. I believe this is a very important matter. When you offer a farmer $20,000 or some other large amount of money I believe that this credit should be protected and the farmer should be protected in whatever way appears to be in his best interests.
Over the years loans were made under the Veterans Land Act with supervision and without supervision, and it was generally conceded that in most instances the supervision was very worth while and a very valuable part of the extension of credit. If this is true, I think it is also necessary for us to try to encourage as many farmers as possible to accept supervision of their operations when they are advanced a loan and we should make the fee for such supervision as reasonable as possible. I believe the amount should not be set by regulation but should be stipulated in the act. I am not one of those who believe that it is difficult to amend statutes. I do not think there is much value in an opposition member moving an amendment but I can do so if that is desired.

We have a minority government now and if I were to move an amendment it would likely pass and the government would have to accept it. Therefore I suggest that the government should bring it in in the first place, if that is the general wish of the committee.
I believe that supervised credit is worth while. It is one of the major features of farm credit and the supervision fee should be as reasonable as possible. We have added a new section to the act which in many instances will result in farmers changing their type of operation from that to which they have been accustomed for a lifetime. A farmer may change from the production of milk for a cheese factory or the production of some other dairy industry commodity, and we are now making certain provisions so that he will be able to borrow money and make the change to a different type of farming operation. I suggest that now more than ever the farmer is going to need a great deal of supervision by duly accredited officials at as reasonable a fee as possible. It is more important now in my opinion than it has been in the past to change our farm credit legislation to provide for supervision. Certain types of loans demand supervision and there is no reason why we should not provide supervision at as low a cost as possible to the individual farmer. I hope that the minister himself will make some suggestion. The fee had been a minimum of $100 or 2 per cent of the amount of the loan. If the minister thinks that $25 is too small, then perhaps he should make a suggestion as to a proper amount.
I really believe, Mr. Chairman, in view of what happened to the last amendment it is not advisable for an opposition member to make an amendment because this will clutter up the field and leave the minister in a position of having to amend our amendment before he can accept it. I hope the minister will give consideration to doing something about the supervisory fee which is in this particular clause.

The borrower shall pay to the corporation an appraisal fee of 2 per cent of the amount of the loan or one hundred dollars, whichever is the lesser,-
This reference is to the appraisal fee. We have already dealt with the apraisal fee in a previous amendment. We are now requested, by at least two parties in the house, to put a maximum on the supervisory fee. speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
We have already passed clause 4 of this bill to amend the Farm Credit Act but I shall have to refer to it in order

to answer these questions. Clause 4 makes it possible for a borrower under part II to take out life insurance. Putting this change into the act makes it optional whether or not a borrower under part II takes out life insurance. Under part III it is mandatory that life insurance be taken out.
I should like to emphasize the importance of this insurance provision in the operations of the Farm Credit Act. One of the difficulties we encounter in trying to help farmers to set up economic units is their reluctance to borrow money, for reasons going back over many years of home and church teaching. This shows up in various ways. In the first place they are reluctant to borrow and then, if they do receive a loan, they think they have been improvident. The protection afforded by life insurance means that one of the great fears in the minds of young couples taking on a large loan has been removed. The fear always existed that should the husband die his wife would be left, possibly with young children, unable to carry on the farm operations alone and saddled with a heavy debt. By making life insurance compulsory for borrowers under part III, which is only available to young people between 21 and 45 years of age, we have been able to eliminate the fear which existed in this respect because, should anything happen to them during the period of their working lives, insurance would take care of the debt and the improved farm could be transferred to their family debt free.
The insurance rates we were able to obtain are very attractive. Most members of this committee would probably be glad to be able to get protection at these rates from such a scheme. I shall put the figures on record so that the committee may know exactly what is paid by those who take out insurance under either the optional section or the compulsory provisions. I will give this table to the Hansard reporter after I have read it. It sets out the annual premium during the total amortization period. As an example, the
Farm Credit Act
premium a young farmer of 21 has to pay each month for a loan of $1,000 is ten cents. So if a farmer takes out a loan of $1,000 his premium would only amount to $1.00 a month during the early period of insurance. It should work out to $12 a year.
Most of us cannot buy insurance of this type at such a price. If the borrower is 25 years of age his premium is still ten cents. If he is 30, it is ten cents; if he is 35, it is 13 cents; if he is 40, it is 22 cents; if he is 45, it is 37 cents; if he is 50, it is 61 cents; if he is 55, it is 94 cents and if he is 61 it is $1.60.
I have been looking into this a little further. If the loan is held for any length of time, the premium goes down. If the loan is held for 29 years, the premium for a year on $1,000 is $1.13; for 25 years it is 98 cents, for 20 years it is 85 cents and for 15 years it is 76 cents. A person who pays 13 cents a month in the initial stages would pay $3.50 a year on a 29-year loan, $2.91 on a 25-year loan, $2.29 on a 20-year loan and $1.79 on a 15-year loan. If a person were 50 years of age he would pay 61 cents a month in the initial stages. Afterwards, on a 29-year loan he would pay $13.85 a year, on a 25-year loan $11.75 a year, on a 20-year loan, $9.48 a year and on a 15-year loan $7.66 a year.
I should like the permission of the committee to put this table in the record as it is, so that hon. members may study it and see how cheap this insurance is to those who make use of it under the terms of this act.

However, there is a very real problem arising out of this particular section. When I was here earlier in the evening it was being discussed and I do not know whether an answer was ever provided. I refer to the intended meaning of the words "in joint tenancy". In the province of Alberta there are two forms under which title may be held by husband and wife, either as joint tenants or tenants in common. The distinction is that if the land is held in the name of husband and wife as joint tenants and not as tenants in common there is title by survivorship. On the death of one spouse it is only necessary for the surviving spouse to obtain a death certificate and file it in the land titles office. Automatically, without the necessity of filing for probate, title will then be changed into the name of the survivor.
On the other hand, joint tenancy is construed to be ownership by each of an individual half interest in the land. I can recall that over the last ten years I have probably drawn several hundred transfers of land and in each instance I have advised my clients to accept the transfer as joint tenants and not as tenants in common. The new subsection 2 of section 26 in clause 7 of the bill reads in part as follows:
.. . where a farmer and his spouse are owners of a farm in joint tenancy . ..

Farm Credit Act
I would submit to the minister that if that is construed strictly it might well in the province of Alberta rule out as ineligible a very large number of husbands and wives who own as joint enants and not as tenants in common. If a sympathetic attitude is adopted and no strict interpretation is made, with the result that the words "joint tenancy" can be extended to cover the thousands of cases which I know exist in the province of Alberta, I think this will meet the situation.

Section 27, which is now being amended by clause 8 of the bill, is the heart and soul of part III of the act. If you are going to have supervised credit, you have to have an understanding with the borrower that he will follow the plan of farm operations approved by the corporation and will permit supervision and from time to time inspection of his farm operation in order that we can assure ourselves that the farm operation is being conducted in such a way the farmer will be able to repay his loan.

Farm Credit Act
Now, what this amendment is doing, and what has been overlooked, is that before the amendment was introduced the borrower was forced to stay under our supervision until he had reduced his loan to 65 per cent of the value of his land. Now, by reason of the amendment, it is 75 per cent. We have put the borrower in this part on the same basis as a part II borrower so that he knows he is not being discriminated against. The farm is a unit, may be worth a great deal of money, but the per acre value of the land may be very low. If this section means what it says, then it seems to me that there may be many areas in which you might have an expensive dairy operation valued at $75,000 while the land may be worth only $100 per acre. If the appraised value of the land is the criteria, then you will have to reduce the loan until there is no loan and it would still not equal 75 per cent of the value of the land.
I feel that the wording should be changed to include the appraised value of the farm operation instead of the appraised value of the land. One of the biggest complaints of the farmers in my area is about land prices. They say the price of the land has no real relationship to the value of the farm as a unit. In most cases the buildings are more expensive than the farm land. Sometimes a dairy herd will be much more expensive than the land. The total farm operation, of course, will be worth more than the land. If the borrower has to reduce the loan to 75 per cent of the appraised value of the land, you are almost asking the borrower to completely wipe out his loan from the corporation. At a certain time a farm improvement loan might be advantageous to the farmer, perhaps after he has made a number of payments on a loan of this type. This loan might 27507-3-117i
