speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the somewhat relaxed atmosphere in committee it is rather difficult to discuss the matter of the amendment which the house has in front of it on third reading. As I was sitting waiting for the debate to be resumed I could not help thinking how short are human memories.
We were told this afternoon that this government had done something that was derogatory to parliament, had done something without authority, and done something concerning which we should have the concurrence of parliament. We are therefore now being castigated and it has been suggested that because of our wrongdoing this bill should now be referred to a committee, based not on the bill but based on actions which, as you pointed out quite correctly in your ruling, were entirely independent of the bill.
I wonder how many hon. members remember the situation with which this nation was confronted in June. I am not going to try to assess responsibility for it at the moment. There will be other times and places when that can be done.
The sooner the better.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The sooner the better. I am not going to deal with that, but at the moment I would like to look at this in a cool, non-partisan fashion rather than in the hysterical fashion of some hon. members. I am not assessing responsibility at the moment,
Customs Tariff
and the responsibility may be dependent on various factors; but there is no doubt that in June the Canadian dollar was subjected to terrific pressure and this nation faced an exchange crisis. The opposition speak of it as if in the cold dawn of a languid morning the government should have dealt with this thing dispassionately and should have consulted parliament, as suggested by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). However, Mr. Speaker, he forgets the fact that there had been an election and that cabinet ministers, like everyone else in the house, were tired. We had just come through a long strenuous campaign. They came back here and were faced with this crisis.

They were no longer
ministers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If you have any more wisecracks stand up and make them, or sit down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Not only do gratuitous remarks interfere with the regular course of debate but I would also direct the attention of the hon. members to the fact that if they are not sitting in their own places they cannot even be heard. I would commend that to their attention as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not want to pursue this matter too far. I was simply saying the government was confronted with that situation immediately after the election. Ministers came back here and faced that situation. We dealt with it; we dealt with it energetically and firmly, as a result of which the crisis was overcome and the exchange fund has been improved. Whatever criticism may be levelled as to responsibility-as I said, Mr. Speaker, I am not going into that question at the moment-I think everyone recognizes the fact that this government dealt with a very difficult situation, dealt with it firmly, dealt with it quickly, dealt with it realistically, as a result of which we are sitting here today in a relatively-and I say "relatively"-good position in so far as the finances of this nation are concerned, and particularly our exchange fund.
This is not only my own assessment of the situation, Mr. Speaker. It was suggested this afternoon that there has been no opportunity to discuss this matter, that no one has reviewed it. I am not going to again refer to the debates in the House of Commons which I mentioned this afternoon. I simply call the attention of hon. members on all sides of the house to the fact that the executive of GATT reviewed this situation within the last two or three weeks and the findings of that organization I tabled in the house the other afternoon. What did they say? GATT

Customs Tariff
said that we, the contracting party, regretted that this action was necessary. Certainly we, as one of the contracting parties, regretted this action. Certainly the Canadian government, ministers returning from an election and any other Canadian would regret the fact that we had to take the action we did take.
We have heard responsible hon. members- particularly one hon. gentleman who has had experience in this House of Commons in days gone by and who since then has been premier of his own province, with heavy responsibilities resting on his own shoulders-talking as nonchalantly and as easily as he did this afternoon about our having disregarded the rights of parliament, as though parliament was something you could start with a push button and then turn off, about concealing things from parliament during those difficult days of June and July. GATT said the contracting party regretted it, and we agreed with that, because we did regret it. GATT said they consulted the international monetary fund, which means, when you look into it, that the I.M.F. agree that this action should have been taken. GATT said there was an undertaking that we would revise or do away with these surcharges as expeditiously as possible. Mind you, there were people and parties-I do not mean political parties, but financial parties and organizations-who did not expect that finding to be made. There were those who suggested in the press and elsewhere that there would be. a time limit placed upon this action; that we would be required within a certain period to do away with certain disciplinary action we had taken. Instead of that GATT accepted our undertaking that we would do away with these measures as expeditiously as possible, that we would report to the council when it meets some time next spring.
There was a review there, Mr. Speaker, and I suggest to hon. gentlemen in this house that if they consider the background of that review and the circumstances under which we were compelled to take this action, it certainly is not appropriate and it is, to put it on a very human basis, not fair to suggest that the government did something which was a reflection on the rights of parliament; that we tried to destroy parliament. When I think of the hours and days which I spent in this house when other people tried to destroy parliament, I find it rather hard to accept that criticism, in view of what prevailed in previous parliaments.
I, personally, in many ways would like to see this amendment adopted. I would like the actions of the government to be reviewed by the banking and commerce committee. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I was told by

someone sitting here a moment ago, who was in the banking and commerce committee meeting this morning, that this was one of the matters on their agenda. I do not know whether that is so. But as I said, in some ways I, personally, would welcome this, because I would like to bring before the banking and commerce committee the evidence which would justify the action this government has taken. If we brought that evidence before that committee, those who are sponsoring this resolution would go away from the committee with their tails between their legs like dogs who had been whipped.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, we are not entirely masters of our own fate in this very closely knit world. The financial situation is such, the exchange situation is such, that something could happen to it. For instance, if the motion of no confidence which was moved by my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) had carried in the house the other evening, and if overnight we had to remove all of these, shall we say, restrictive actions which this government has taken, I suggest that the reaction on the exchange fund and on the Canadian dollar would make the storm of last June look like a summer shower and we would have been in a much worse situation than we were. If we had not taken this action in June, if the government had sat back, if we had summoned parliament, for instance, as is suggested-and in many ways we would have liked to summon parliament-within a week after the election, because of the uncertain political situation I think the Canadian dollar would have been at 50 cents or less. It was essential that this action be taken. We have taken it. We are prepared to stand on the record.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I would like to have it reviewed by a committee. I am not sure what the reaction would be outside of this nation if we agreed to such action at the moment. There might be a reaction, in view of the delicate situation which prevails, and because of the uncertain political situation alone. We have been talking about an election which sometimes comes over the horizon. If there were an election in the immediate future, in view of the uncertain situation, in view of the uncertainty that developed after June 18, an uncertainty which I think largely precipitated a run on the dollar-and it has been said time and again recently that hon. members opposite would welcome another election-I do not know what would happen in the present situation.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is my responsibility to conserve the financial situation, to avoid any crisis which might develop, to avoid any run on the dollar and to maintain

the financial integrity of this nation: and that this government is determined to do as long as it is responsible for the financial affairs of the nation. Therefore all I can say at the moment is that I very much regret the fact that an hon. gentleman with long years of experience in administration, and the record he has of responsibility as a premier, and knowing the responsibilities with which people in public life are faced, particularly those on the treasury benches for the time being, felt it necessary to move the motion he has moved this evening. He wants a review of this matter. He can have a review in almost any way he suggests, provided it is not one which attacks the integrity of the financial position of this country and the position of the government on these matters for which we are responsible.
Mr. Speaker, our estimates will be before the house before long. There are a dozen ways in which this matter can be dealt with. I suggest to the hon. member, even yet, that he should withdraw his amendment and we should pass this bill which, after all, as far as the financial structure is concerned, is a minor matter. We have all agreed on that. It is only a small section. It is not the bill, though, Mr. Speaker; it is the implications of the amendment which has been moved and which is before us, which suggests that all the financial measures which this government has taken should be reviewed and perhaps discarded, and that-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I hear somebody saying,
"Hear, hear". If that were done, the financial situation of this nation would be a very serious one indeed. I am again asking the hon. member to withdraw this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am much more impressed with the tone and temper of what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) has said since dinner than with what he said before dinner, and I think the whole house has been impressed in the same way. I will try to make my contribution, as far as I can, in the same vein. I am rising to support the motion moved by the hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam, and I think the arguments put forward by the minister are the best possible support for it.
If what the minister says is correct, if the financial situation of this country is as precarious as the minister has just portrayed it as being, then there is the utmost need for complete unanimity in the parliament of this country. It seems to me that the minister misapprehends what we understand by
Customs Tariff
responsible government when he says parliament is not to be trusted to consider these matters. All the motion seeks to do is to send this bill to a committee. The minister suggests that all sorts of dire consequences would follow from such a course. If there were any dire consequences, those consequences, I suggest, would be on the heads of those who were irresponsible enough to bring them about. I doubt if the minister was seriously suggesting that his colleagues here in the House of Commons are a lot of irresponsible people. If he was, I think the minister is more of an old fashioned pre-Responsible Government Tory than I had thought him to be.
Let me make this clear. We did not criticize the government for acting in the emergency. My hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) took a position in June which, perhaps, some of his partisan friends thought was not partisan enough. I was not one of them. I agreed completely with the position he took. His statements can be read by any hon. member who cares to do so, and some hon. members ought to read them instead of indulging in the foolish and untrue statements they frequently make about these matters. Notwithstanding the fact that extraordinary action was taken in a way we thought, and still think, was unconstitutional and perhaps illegal, my hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition, confined himself to saying that the most important thing was to safeguard the value of the Canadian dollar and that he, and those associated with him, would not do anything to lessen the effectiveness of the steps taken by the government in that regard. But one thing he said should not be forgotten. Speaking as a Liberal, he said: parliament should be called as soon as possible to deal with these matters.
That is what should have been done. I can go back to the analogy with 1947 which the government is always using. That is what the government of that day did. The government of that day was faced with an emergency when parliament was not sitting, but my friend Mr. Abbott who was minister of finance at that time went on the air and announced that parliament, when called, was going to be asked to enact legislation to provide for certain taxes but that the Department of National Revenue was authorized to collect them immediately. However, they would be placed before parliament. I have the documents right in my hand if anyone would like me to read them, but I prefer not to take the time. Mr. Abbott said in parliament: I did not impose those taxes. I have no right to do so, but I did give fair warning

Customs Tariff
to the people that we were going to ask parliament to have the taxes made retroactive, and we have a majority.
The bill which is before us right now is a bill which imposes taxes-taxes which have been imposed since April 10 as a result of a statement made by the hon. gentleman's predecessor. And what did the hon. gentleman's predecessor, or the chief of the hon. gentleman's predecessor, do? He did not give parliament a chance to deal with this matter. He had parliament dissolved. The consequence was the election of the kind of parliament we have now, where the minister is very unsure whether he can get his bill through at all. That is the difference between the situation in which Mr. Abbott found himself in 1947 and the situation in which the government finds itself with respect to this bill. I am not talking about the surcharges, but about the bill itself. These charges have been imposed since April.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question so that there may be no confusion at all? The bill which is presently before us does not impose any taxes whatever, because it reduces taxes. Is that not the case?

I do not think there is any difference. It does not matter whether taxation is increased or reduced. It is the imposition of a tax. I might point out to the minister that if this bill does not pass, his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, would have to instruct his officials to go back and collect all the back taxes on the old basis if, in fact, this bill does reduce taxes, because that would be the law. The law has not been enforced since April.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Can the hon. gentleman point to one clause in this bill which imposes a tax?

If it is clearly understood that I have the same latitude as to time as has the minister, I would be glad to deal with that point, but I do not think it is a very important point compared to some of the other matters which have been raised.
Caught out.
I might remind hon. gentlemen opposite that I listened to the minister without a single interruption of any kind.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was hoping we would not get any more interruptions. The minister was accorded a courteous reception by the house and I think the hon. member is entitled to the same, as are all hon. members.

I would remind hon. members, some of whom may have forgotten, that these surcharges were imposed not by radio

but by television, because we have moved with the times. The Prime Minister had this to say-I am reading from the words he used that night:
It is natural to expect that the measures taken will be discussed by parliament when it meets.
There were some of us who took the Prime Minister at his word and who expected to find in the speech from the throne words similar to those found in the speech from the throne in 1947. Here is what was said in the speech from the throne in December 1947:
Provision of a temporary character has been made to conserve and supplement Canada's reserve of United States dollars. The measures recently announced to deal with the various aspects of the immediate foreign exchange difficulty will be submitted for your approval.
That is the attitude of a government which considers itself responsible to parliament. What we are complaining about is that we now have a government which boasts that it has no responsibility to parliament, a government which boasts that parliament should not be allowed to look at what it is doing, a government which says that parliament should have nothing to say about the imposition of taxes; that the verdict of the people last June should be disregarded entirely. That is just what the Minister of Finance has said this evening-that the views of parliament should be disregarded entirely, that the distortion and, in our view, the misuse of statutes enacted for another purpose should be a cloak to impose taxes and that parliament should not have any chance to consider them.
I,	personally, would have been willing to forgive the government for using any device it might have found to hand to meet the crisis of last June, though I think it would have been better to have followed the example of Mr. Abbott and to call parliament as soon as possible in order that parliament might deal with the matter. That would have been a better and more constitutional way of doing things but, as I say, I personally would have said that in a crisis such as arose last summer, whatever measures needed to be taken should be taken and the government of the day should carry them out. What I complain about and what, I conceive, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and those associated with him in putting forward this motion complain about is that this government, though in a minority, did not come as quickly as possible to parliament to say: "The elected representatives of the people have the sole right to tax in this country. This is a tax and we ask you to co-operate with us in dealing with this national emergency."

That is what should have been done, and if it had, I suggest that the government would have had the opportunity to present the good case which the minister boasted it had. The minister said he would like to bring the evidence before us. Well, we should have liked to have it. Is the minister suggesting that there is any member of this house who, given the evidence, would be so unpatriotic that he would not do what was in the national interest? Is that the view that the minister takes of the members of this house? Because it is not the view that I take, and I do not believe it is the view the majority of the members take.
Now, sir, I feel I should very briefly point out what the effect, as I understand it, of this amendment would be. This amendment does not kill the bill. Except in a very temporary way it does not even interfere with its progress. During the time that it may be under consideration in the banking and commerce committee, if the hon. member's amendment is accepted, the tax structure will carry on in exactly the same way as it has since April 10. Nothing will be changed outside this house. There is no urgency, in that sense, about passing the bill, none at all. What it would do is to enable the minister and his officials to come before the committee and, as the minister himself said he would like to do, tell us what the real situation is, tell us what the real problems are, and tell us what really ought to be done to meet this situation. I am perfectly sure that if the minister and the government are willing to trust the members of the house to do their duty as Canadians, they will not be disappointed. Therefore, sir, for the reason that it will not kill the bill, for the reason that it will not defeat the government, and for the reason that all it will do is to give to parliament the right to scrutinize taxation, I ask that this amendment be accepted.
Mind you, I think it is second best even at that. I think it would be much better if we had a bill before us and parliament determined these things right here. The minister talked about discussions on his estimates, and other opportunities of that sort. We want the right, as the elected representatives of the people, not just to discuss but to determine these matters. We are the ones who have the right to determine them, not a handful of half discredited ministers sitting in the cabinet. I say that because the government has failed to act in a responsible fashion, and I use that term in its correct constitutional sense. It has failed properly to discharge its responsibility to the elected
Customs Tariff
representatives of the people and to bring a tax measure before us. We have sought by one means or another open to us under the-rules to bring this matter before the house in some fashion in which hon. members could get at it and could find out what was really needed in the national interest, and find out how much was really needed in the national interest. While I am sure the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would consider this a second best, it is still a great deal better than having parliament totally ignored and bypassed, and refused any opportunity to consider $200 million of taxation imposed by television and order in council by a Prime Minister who, on Dominion day of 1960, talked about other taxes raised by order in council and said that that was not going to happen any more. I suggest that all hon. members read the passage which was read by the hon. member for York-Humber this afternoon as reported at pages 5648 and 5649 of Hansard, where the Prime Minister gave the most categorical of undertakings that never again in this country would taxes be imposed by order in council. Not two years had passed when on June 24 there was imposed $200 million of taxation by order in council, the like of which has never happened before in Canada at any time, or perhaps in any other country where the British system of responsible government prevails. For that reason, sir, because we believe in responsible government, I am happy indeed to support the amendment of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.

speakeroldname: Mr. Heward Graffley (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, just last week the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) said in this house: "We are here to defeat this government". I fully realized when elected last June 18 that I came to support a minority government, but I felt that opposition tactics would be tactics based on principles. I knew the opposition would bring votes to the floor of this house one way or the other to try to defeat a minority government. But what do we see? Last week, putting party before country, the hon. member for Essex East said that the only thing he had to do here was to defeat the government.
Shame.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Since the official opposition and the party to my far right do not seem to be able to accomplish this on matters of' principle, we see before us fractious procedural debates. The hon. member who was just spoken knows that this amendment and:

this particular procedure on third reading is very extraordinary. I think it is all the more extraordinary that this whole debate is taking place when the hon. member realizes full well that in another place today we agreed, and I thought agreed in a bipartisan manner, to bring forward the type of subject that the hon. member wants to have discussed. I felt that his remarks on the floor of this house, after what went on in another place today, were slightly hollow when we consider the good fellowship which took place in the other place; and I say that in all sincerity. If hon. members opposite wanted to discuss in committee particular matters pertaining to this bill, which does not have the wide significance they would like to attach to it, or if there were any doubts relating to surcharge matters then I suggest those doubts were fully explained by my minister during the committee stage in relation to items 440m and 440n. They agreed that these matters were explained. Therefore it becomes quite apparent that all hon. members want to discuss, if this bill is put back into committee, is something which is not germane at all to the bill. They want to discuss the broad and general topic of surcharges. I think they would have been much more forthright with the house if they had come out and said that rather than proceed- Mr. Speaker: Order. It is now ten o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow, which is one of the short days, I thought the house might consider six items standing in the name of the Minister of Justice and take them in this order. Four of them are resolutions, which of course could pass rather quickly and then the bills would be before us later on. The first item would be Bill No. C-49, to amend an act to amend the Combines Investigation Act. The second is resolution No. 25 on today's order paper, to amend the Judges Act. The third resolution is No. 26, to amend the Admiralty Act. The fourth is the resolution which is No. 22 on today's order paper, a measure to amend the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act, then, fifth, Bill No. C-48 which deals with the revision and consolidation of the Interpretation Act, and No. 6, the resolution dealing with the Revised Statutes of Canada.
On Thursday or Friday we propose dealing with the resolution respecting a national development board. It will depend on certain arrangements I have to make with the Minister of Finance.
